sources.name: Canaltech
sources.title: Carga milionária de RTX 5090 desaparece misteriosamente no aeroporto de Guarulhos
sources.text: Por Raphael Giannotti | 19/10/2026 às 10:32 A RTX 5090 é uma placa de vídeo cobiçada, principalmente por causa do seu potencial em IA. Ela é tão cobiçada que, do nada, uma carga inteira dessa GPU, modelos da Zotac, sumiu logo que chegou ao Aeroporto Internacional de Guarulhos , em São Paulo, segundo a própria distribuidora Oderço, que fica no Paraná. O prejuízo passa de R$ 2.000.000 , imagina se fosse uma versão banhada a ouro . Nas redes sociais, Oderço Matos, presidente da distribuidora, disse que, em mais de 38 anos de história da empresa, com 18 anos realizando importações, nunca havia perdido uma carga . "Recentemente, dois pallets de mercadoria chegaram ao Aeroporto Internacional de Guarulhos. E lá dentro, sumiram", relata o empresário. Não foi dito quantas placas sumiram, mas dois pallets somam, facilmente, algumas centenas de unidades, podendo passar de 400 se considerarmos caixas avulsas para o varejo. De qualquer forma, o prejuízo é de R$ 2.500.000 , principalmente porque o preço de uma RTX 5090 não é nada baixo hoje em dia por causa da crise. O presidente da distribuidora relata que não tem qualquer informação sobre o que pode ter levado ao sumiço dessas caixas . Oderço até critica a falta de comunicação pelo aeroporto, que tem câmeras espalhadas por todos os lados para a segurança do ambiente, já que por lá passam mais de 120 mil pessoas por dia e muitas toneladas de carga são transportadas diariamente. No Brasil, uma RTX 5090 da Zotac custa, em média, R$ 35.000 . Vale lembrar que esse é o valor repassado ao consumidor no varejo e não o que uma distribuidora paga. A GeForce RTX 5090, em geral, está virando uma lenda na indústria. Não por causa de sua capacidade de processamento, mas porque ela está sumindo do mercado aos poucos . Em games, ela é a melhor disponível hoje para quem pode investir dezenas de milhares de reais. Porém ela também é muito útil em processamento de inteligência artificial por conta do chip robusto e de 32 GB de memória de vídeo. No ano passado, antes do boom da IA, uma RTX 5090 chegou a custar pouco menos de R$ 15.000 , dependendo do modelo e da loja. Menos de seis meses depois, ela já custava muito mais e isso não aconteceu só no Brasil, mas em todo o mundo .

sources.name: Tecmundo
sources.title: Carga de GPUs RTX 5090 avaliada em R$ 2,5 milhões desaparece no Aeroporto de Guarulhos
sources.text: Notebooks com RTX Spark terão centenas de jogos no lançamento Call of Duty em 2027! Veja teste A Nvidia e a Microsoft apresentaram o Surface Ultra, novo notebook ultrafino baseado na tecnologia RTX Spark. O modelo é um dos primeiros adotar a tecnologia, q. Uma carga de GPUs RTX 5090 da Zotac desapareceu após chegar ao Aeroporto Internacional de São Paulo, em Guarulhos (SP), recentemente, de acordo com a Oderço Distribuidora. O conteúdo que sumiu é avaliado em cerca de R$ 2,5 milhões, considerando o preço de custo . Em vídeo divulgado no perfil oficial da companhia no Instagram, no último sábado (17), o empresário Oderço Matos, presidente da empresa, afirma que dois pallets contendo as unidades da placa de vídeo sumiram assim que desembarcaram em Guarulhos . Ele também cobrou explicações da concessionária que administra o aeroporto. Ao TecMundo, a GRU Airport informou que “vem empenhando todos os esforços” para solucionar o caso desde que tomou conhecimento do sumiço da carga (veja mais detalhes abaixo). Atuando no ramo há mais de 38 anos, dos quais 18 anos com importações, o presidente da distribuidora relata que esta foi a primeira vez que perdeu uma carga . Sem fornecer maiores detalhes de como o sumiço aconteceu, ele criticou a falta de respostas da administradora do aeroporto. Ele não informou a quantidade exata de GPUs RTX 5090 da Zotac que desapareceram em Guarulhos. No entanto, ressaltou que se trata de uma das placas de vídeo mais cobiçadas do mercado , devido ao uso em soluções de inteligência artificial, principalmente, e também em PCs de jogos. Com 32 GB GDDR7 de memória de vídeo, arquitetura Blackwell da Nvidia e 28 Gbps de velocidade, o modelo em questão tem preço médio de R$ 35 mil no Brasil , atualmente. O valor cobrado disparou nos últimos meses devido à alta demanda relacionada à IA. Além de informar o sumiço às autoridades competentes e colaborar com a investigação, a concessionária disse que mantém contato com o importador e repassou as orientações para o início do processo de indenização . Confira a nota da GRU Airport enviada ao TecMundo: “ A GRU Airport informa que, desde que tomou conhecimento do ocorrido, vem empenhando todos os esforços para solucioná-lo. A não localização da carga já foi formalmente reportada às autoridades competentes para apoio nas investigações. Paralelamente, nossa equipe de atendimento ao cliente mantém contato constante com o representante do importador. Em 14/10/2026, diante do tempo decorrido, foram transmitidas as orientações necessárias para o início do processo de indenização, em conformidade com os procedimentos vigentes. No momento, a concessionária aguarda a apresentação da documentação por parte do cliente para análise e finalização do processo. Adicionalmente, o departamento jurídico da empresa prestará todo o suporte necessário para o desfecho do caso ”. Nos EUA, uma loja está obrigando os clientes a assinarem um termo concordando em não exportar a RTX 5090 adquirida. Saiba mais detalhes nesta matéria . stories.title: EUA mandam banir o uso da IA DeepSeek dos sistemas de TI governamentais
stories.summary: Medida vem um dia depois de a chinesa DeepSeek anunciar uma atualização do seu modelo de IA que promete concluir tarefas mais rapidamente e gerar respostas mais curtas.

sources.name: Convergencia Digital
sources.title: EUA mandam banir o uso da IA DeepSeek dos sistemas de TI governamentais
sources.text: O governo dos Estados Unidos declarou guerra à inteligência artificial chinesa DeepSeek. O Departamento de Segurança Interna dos EUA determinou a remoção de produtos da empresa— bem como de serviços de terceiros que utilizam esse modelo de inteligência artificial chinês — dos sistemas de TI de agências civis norte-americanas, conforme um comunicado publicado na segunda-feira, 19/10. O departamento também proibiu que agências governamentais civis dos EUA adquiram produtos da DeepSeek ou serviços de terceiros desenvolvidos com o uso dessa tecnologia. O Departamento de Segurança Interna afirmou que os modelos da DeepSeek apresentam “múltiplos vetores de ameaça” e expressou preocupação de que o uso desses produtos “possa resultar na transferência de dados sensíveis para a República Popular da China, caso sejam utilizados por funcionários ou fornecedores do governo norte-americano”. A reação chega dois dias depois de a DeepSeek lançar uma atualização de seu modelo de inteligência artificial que promete concluir tarefas mais rapidamente e gerar respostas mais curtas. A proposta é reduzir o tempo de espera e o custo de uso, ao mesmo tempo em que melhora o desempenho do sistema. Batizada de V4.1-Flash-1017, a versão já está disponível no site, no aplicativo e na plataforma para desenvolvedores da empresa chinesa. DeepSeek relata avanços em raciocínio, programação, compreensão de imagens e tarefas executadas por agentes de IA. A DeepSeek informa ainda que na tabela oficial, o milhão de tokens gerados custa US$ 0,60 fora do horário de pico e US$ 1,20 no pico. Para a entrada de informações sem reaproveitamento de cache, os valores são de US$ 0,15 e US$ 0,30, respectivamente.

sources.name: Olhar Digital IA
sources.title: EUA mandam banir inteligência artificial DeepSeek de redes federais
sources.text: O Departamento de Segurança Interna dos Estados Unidos (DHS) determinou que órgãos civis federais removam tecnologias de inteligência artificial da chinesa DeepSeek de seus sistemas de TI. A ordem também proíbe novas aquisições de produtos e serviços da empresa. A restrição inclui ferramentas de empresas afiliadas e serviços de terceiros desenvolvidos com base na tecnologia da DeepSeek . O governo americano aponta riscos à segurança de dados, mas não estabeleceu um prazo para a retirada. A determinação foi emitida com base na Lei de Segurança da Cadeia de Suprimentos de Aquisições Federais, de 2018, após uma análise do Conselho Federal de Segurança de Aquisições. Segundo o DHS, os modelos de IA da DeepSeek apresentam “múltiplos vetores de ameaça”. O departamento teme que o uso dessas ferramentas por funcionários públicos ou fornecedores resulte na transferência de informações sensíveis para a China . O órgão também afirma que a tecnologia poderia produzir informações de inteligência sobre cidadãos americanos e agências governamentais. Outra preocupação é a possibilidade de os próprios modelos conterem programas maliciosos ou vulnerabilidades de segurança. A proibição não se limita aos produtos da empresa chinesa: serviços de terceiros que utilizam implementações de seus modelos também estão sujeitos à medida. A decisão federal amplia as restrições que já vinham sendo adotadas nos Estados Unidos. O Departamento de Comércio e a Marinha haviam proibido o uso da DeepSeek em dispositivos oficiais. Nova York, Tennessee e Virgínia também adotaram medidas semelhantes. Em um memorando de julho, divulgado na segunda-feira, 19 de outubro, o DHS orientou as agências federais a monitorar o tráfego de dados que entra e sai dos sites governamentais. A iniciativa busca identificar possíveis riscos associados ao uso da tecnologia. Entre as medidas adotadas ou propostas pelos Estados Unidos contra tecnologias chinesas estão: As iniciativas fazem parte de uma política mais ampla de contenção de riscos associados à tecnologia chinesa. Segundo o material de origem, 82% dos eletrônicos dos Estados Unidos eram testados na China no ano passado. Até a divulgação das informações, a Embaixada da China em Washington não havia comentado a decisão envolvendo a DeepSeek. Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

stories.title: Sullivan & Cromwell brings legal expertise into agreement review
stories.summary: In collaboration with OpenAI, Sullivan & Cromwell developed Agreement Analyzer, an AI tool for identifying issues in a draft agreement.

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: Sullivan & Cromwell brings legal expertise into agreement review
sources.text: In collaboration with OpenAI, Sullivan & Cromwell developed Agreement Analyzer, an AI tool for identifying issues in a draft agreement. For lawyers at Sullivan & Cromwell, reviewing a draft agreement includes weighing its terms against relevant precedents, using approaches based on the Firm’s experience and being mindful of a client’s priorities. The firm’s Agreement Analyzer brings those inputs into a single review workflow, producing analysis and proposed changes that lawyers can inspect and refine. Though AI was initially used most for repetitive, administrative tasks like drafting email responses or checking calendars, Savva finds that recent improvements in AI models’ analytical capabilities have changed its usage. “Now, we’re seeing many more opportunities for use in challenging legal tasks such as deep analysis of complex agreements,” he says. Agreement Analyzer helps lawyers compare corresponding provisions across precedents and track how those provisions interact. Sullivan & Cromwell partner John Savva developed Agreement Analyzer as a single-user proof of concept built with Codex. He then collaborated with OpenAI on improving the quality of outputs, enhancing efficiency through parallel processing and transforming the application into a tool that could be used by multiple lawyers at the same time. Agreement Analyzer integrates Sullivan & Cromwell’s workflows, curated firm precedents, negotiating playbooks and ChatGPT Enterprise. After inputting a draft agreement into the tool, a lawyer can add their own selected precedents and a playbook with firm and client positions, as well as information on market practice. The tool performs multiple review cycles from different perspectives, synthesizes the outputs, helps identify potential issues and returns a memorandum and proposed tracked changes for a lawyer to review, adapt or reject. Savva emphasizes that what makes an AI tool’s output trustworthy is full transparency. “If an AI tool makes a claim about market practice, you need to be able to see the source of that information,” he says. Savva describes an application in which agents develop conclusions and other agents challenge them in an adversarial process. In a potential use case, specialized agents review the agreement in parallel for such things as market deviations and risk allocation, interactions between clauses, and ambiguities that could impact litigation. The results distinguish findings supported after challenge by other agents, dismissed findings, and unverified issues retained with qualifications. Lawyers can inspect the issues, their supporting explanations, and the relevant precedents, then decide which findings warrant changes in the final markup. Sullivan & Cromwell is continuing to explore tools shaped around specific legal tasks. For Savva, stronger analytical capabilities create an opportunity to support more of the research and writing process. Savva points to advances in reasoning capabilities with GPT‑6 Astra: “Astra’s really moved things forward in terms of the quality of the reasoning that’s available, and that has been the bottleneck in the past,” he says.

stories.title: Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

sources.name: Hugging Face
sources.title: Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers
sources.text: Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control . You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move. Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection : You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now! Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder): Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image: FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height , width , or num_inference_steps to change them. Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want , with the change included. With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image : Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id , a bbox , and a desc , and the caption mentions it as . Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max] , y first , on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size. For edits, each region says where its content comes from ( src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes ( tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is. This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire: Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning ). Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4 . Load any of them with from_single_file , then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too. For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config . FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit ). Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd : To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags: --gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit. A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora . More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README . For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script ( train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py ) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as . See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example. In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models. End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup: Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend. A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens: FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2. The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels. So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch , and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size. The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072. This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call. The transformer processes the tokens in two stages: The two stages differ in who can attend to whom . In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them. At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which

sources.name: Apple Machine Learning
sources.title: Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio
sources.text: Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post , we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators. In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model â Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters â right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see Figure 1 ), well above average human reading speed. Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio. We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on Mac Studio , using the MLX LM package, as described in our prior post . We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads. We evaluate three frontier-class models ( Table 1 ) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts â and thus parameters â active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively). Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with mlx_lm.benchmark . For example, running Qwen 3.8 with 8,192 tokens of context and generating 128 tokens is performed with the command line: A popular use of local LLMs on Mac Studio is running agentic experiences in a private environment, including agentic coding applications that often need large contexts. We therefore report performance at both 8,192 and 65,536 context sizes. Raw TTFT and decode throughput are reported in Table 2 and Table 3 , respectively. Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup. In Figure 2 , we compare their inference performance on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, both on M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra. Time to first token (TTFT) is essentially compute bound, and that is where the Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU shine: the specialized hardware support for fast matrix-multiplication of the GPU Neural Accelerator directly translates into significant speedups for TTFT, up to 4.6Ã faster compared to an M3 Ultra (see Figure 2 ). That makes the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra the desktop of choice when it comes to handling tasks involving very large contexts. Generation speed (in tokens per second) is memory-bandwidth bound. The M5 Ultra chip delivers 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, up from 819 GB/s for the M3 Ultra. Here again, that translates directly into generation speed (see Figure 3 ), with the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra reporting 1.6Ã faster tokens/s. The Mac Studio is also energy-efficient for LLM inference (see Figure 4 ): peak power consumption is about 200W for the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, and 300W for the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra â a fraction of the power used by a common toaster. More importantly, that modest amount of power consumption means a Mac Studio can be deployed for AI work in any home or office environment. While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers. Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the modelâs inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the modelâs layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see Figure 5 ) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes. MLX supports different parallelization schemes, as described in the MLX distributed documentation . These rely on fast inter-machine communication: macOS 26.2 introduced a low-latency RDMA driver over Thunderbolt 5, and MLX (v0.30.1 and later) builds on top of this driver and provides new communication collectives ( jaccl , pronounced âjackalâ) for different parallelization schemes. In our setup, the two Mac Studios are connected with two Thunderbolt cables (to double the link bandwidth), providing the RDMA-over-Thunderbolt link that jaccl uses. sources.name: Apple Machine Learning
sources.title: Selection-Based Structured Reasoning: Toward Efficient Multimodal Search Agents
sources.text: Selection-Based Structured Reasoning: Toward Efficient Multimodal Search Agents Authors Feiyu Gavin Zhuâ **, Xiaoyu Zhu, Jiqi Yang, Rui Yangâ¡***, Arnab Kumar Mondal, Yancheng Wang, Xinke Deng, Jean Ohâ , Reid Simmonsâ , Joerg Liebelt, Xiang Kong, Zhongyu Jiang Multimodal agents commonly generate freeform reasoning before each action. For small models, limited model capacity can result in lengthy reasoning that provides little useful guidance for action generation while incurring substantial inference cost. To address this challenge, we introduce Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR), a framework that reformulates reasoning as selection instead of open-ended generation. SSR represents recurring high-level reasoning as pre-specified, reusable natural-language candidates. At each turn, the model selects from the reasoning candidates based on their likelihoods given the current context, without an auxiliary task head. Using pre-specified reasoning traces enables parallel scoring, where teacher-forced prefilling computes token likelihoods concurrently within and across candidates using a shared context KV cache. We evaluated SSR on seven multimodal search benchmarks using 2B and 4B models. Across multiple reinforcement learning objectives and supervised fine-tuning, SSR delivers significant efficiency gains without sacrificing task performance. SSR achieves an average success rate competitive with leading search agents of the same scale, while reducing per-turn reasoning latency by over 90% and total per-question model inference latency by 28â54%. Learning Structured Reasoning via Tractable Trajectory Control July 2, 2026 research area Computer Vision , research area Speech and Natural Language Processing conference ICML Large language models can exhibit emergent reasoning behaviors, often manifested as recurring lexical patterns (e.g., âwait,â indicating verification). However, complex reasoning trajectories remain sparse in unconstrained sampling, and standard RL often fails to guarantee the acquisition of diverse reasoning behaviors. We propose a systematic discovery and reinforcement of diverse reasoning patterns through structured reasoning, a paradigm thatâ¦ Interleaved Reasoning for Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning May 28, 2025 research area Knowledge Bases and Search , research area Speech and Natural Language Processing Long chain-of-thought (CoT) significantly enhances large language modelsâ (LLM) reasoning capabilities. However, the extensive reasoning traces lead to inefficiencies and an increased time-to-first-token (TTFT). We propose a novel training paradigm that uses reinforcement learning (RL) to guide reasoning LLMs to interleave thinking and answering for multi-hop questions. We observe that models inherently possess the ability to perform interleavedâ¦ Our research in machine learning breaks new ground every day.
